query: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo is a disordered BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with a room-temperature compressive yield strength of 1719 MPa, but its high Mo content increases the electronegativity difference and is associated with reduced plasticity. What single intervention could improve its room-temperature compressive strength–plasticity balance without sacrificing its high strength? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, the operative mechanism, the predicted change in strength and plasticity relative to the equiatomic disordered-BCC alloy, the conditions and limits under which the effect should occur, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a very small amount of interstitial carbon (~0.1 at.%) into the equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo disordered BCC alloy will generate a fine dispersion of coherent carbide nanoprecipitates that subtly modify the local bonding environment. This modification is expected to slightly alter the stacking fault energy and promote extra dislocation mobility and/or twinning (i.e., activating TWIP/TRIP-like mechanisms) so that the alloy retains its high compressive yield strength while displaying considerably improved plasticity.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo disordered BCC refractory high-entropy alloy. Its high Mo content creates a larger average electronegativity difference that underlies its high yield strength (~1719 MPa) but also limits plasticity.
generation.intervention: Introduce ~0.1 at.% interstitial carbon during alloy synthesis (e.g., via vacuum arc melting) to dope the alloy.
generation.conditions: The alloy should be produced under controlled melting and cooling conditions at ambient pressure to retain the disordered BCC phase. Carbon content must be kept low to avoid extensive carbide network formation; the goal is to promote a dispersion of nanoscale, coherent carbide precipitates.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of nanoscale carbide precipitates (likely based on Ti or Zr carbides) that remain coherent with the BCC matrix provides local regions of modified bonding. These precipitates serve as both obstacles and sources altering dislocation behavior.
generation.mechanism: Interstitial carbon atoms modify the local lattice environment by reducing the effective electronegativity difference, thereby slightly changing stacking fault energies and increasing the activity of dislocation motion and/or twinning. The coherent carbide precipitates also provide precipitation strengthening that pins dislocations without ‘locking’ them completely, thus enhancing plasticity without a loss in yield strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the undoped alloy, the carbon-doped alloy will exhibit a similar or slightly enhanced compressive yield strength (~1700 MPa) while showing a significantly higher compressive plastic strain (e.g., increased by a factor of ~2, though exact numbers are uncertain) leading to a better strength–plasticity balance.
generation.baseline: The current equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo alloy, with a disordered BCC structure, exhibits a compressive yield strength of 1719 MPa but limited plasticity due to the effects of high Mo content.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected only when the carbon addition is kept to a minimal level (~0.1 at.%) to ensure that carbide formation is fine and coherent. Exceeding this level may promote coarse carbides that could embrittle the alloy. This intervention is also applicable under processing regimes that maintain the disordered BCC matrix (ambient pressure and controlled cooling).
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis extrapolates from results reported in studies on interstitially alloyed HEAs that activate TWIP/TRIP mechanisms (e.g., PMC5227964) and from low‐concentration carbide formation work (e.g., PMC7517255). The exact carbide phase, particle distribution, and quantitative enhancement of plasticity in NbZrTiHfMo are not yet verified and remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of NbZrTiHfMo alloy samples using identical processing conditions, with one set doped with approximately 0.1 at.% carbon and the other set undoped as a control. Characterize both sets using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to confirm that the single disordered BCC phase persists and to detect the presence (and morphology) of nanoscale carbide precipitates. Conduct room-temperature compressive tests to evaluate yield strength and plastic strain.
measurements: Microstructural analysis via TEM and XRD (phase and precipitate characterization)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the carbon-doped alloy either shows a significant drop in compressive yield strength or does not exhibit a measurable improvement in plasticity (i.e. if its plastic strain remains similar to or lower than that of the undoped alloy), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractHigh-entropy alloys (HEAs) consisting of multiple principle elements provide an avenue for realizing exceptional mechanical, physical and chemical properties. We report a novel strategy for designing a new class of HEAs incorporating the additional interstitial element carbon. This results in joint activation of twinning- and transformation-induced plasticity (TWIP and TRIP) by tuning the matrix phase’s instability in a metastable TRIP-assisted dual-phase HEA. Besides TWIP and TRIP, such alloys benefit from massive substitutional and interstitial solid solution strengthening as well as from the composite effect associated with its dual-phase structure. Nanosize particle formation and grain size reduction are also utilized. The new interstitial TWIP-TRIP-HEA thus unifies all metallic strengthening mechanisms in one material, leading to twice the tensile strength compared to a single-phase HEA with similar composition, yet, at identical ductility.

In this work, the formation of carbide with the concertation of carbon at 0.1 at.% in refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) Mo15Nb20Re15Ta30W20 was studied under both ambient and high-pressure high-temperature conditions. The x-ray diffraction of dilute carbon (C)-doped RHEA under ambient pressure showed that the phases and lattice constant of RHEA were not influenced by the addition of 0.1 at.% C. In contrast, C-doped RHEA showed unexpected phase formation and transformation under combined high-pressure and high-temperature conditions by resistively employing the heated diamond anvil cell (DAC) technique. The new FCC_L12 phase appeared at 6 GPa and 809 °C and preserved the ambient temperature and pressure. High-pressure and high-temperature promoted the formation of carbides Ta3C and Nb3C, which are stable and may further improve the mechanical performance of the dilute C-doped alloy Mo15Nb20Re15Ta30W20.
